top_choice_rationale: P003 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) credits one achievement, how technology and trade change the demand for skills, tasks and local labour. Katz's skill-demand and task framework is the conceptual half. The Autor-Hanson local-labour-market designs are the empirical half. The work is two to three decades old and has been replicated, qualified and contested without being overturned. Its finding of slow, uneven and persistent adjustment matches the long-run historical record on railways and electrification. The citation should claim the evidence and the framework as developed by these laureates, not originate the task model, which also owes much to Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu. I rank P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) a close second. Dorn's co-authorship of the import-shock papers gives it cleaner attribution, and I would not oppose it on scientific grounds. I judge the Goldin overlap with Katz's strand thematic rather than substantive, so I weigh the framework strand more than P001's backers do. I place P004 third because the cross-country constitutional evidence is more weakly identified, and Besley's share is the least separable. I place P002 fourth. BLP is a durable method that changed what regulators can measure, but its credit set is wider than three names and it is a method rather than a finding. I rank no award last because every proposed prize rests on mature, substantive work. Support counts are not treated as evidence of merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. I have no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz, Dorn, Persson, Tabellini, Besley, Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes. My research on electrification, railways and labour is thematically adjacent to P003 and P001, and my economic-history background may colour my reading of the Goldin overlap. I have collegial ties at Lund to committee members Andersson and Teorell (formerly at Lund), who are members rather than candidates. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
